newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich victory seen despite defections.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich victory seen despite defections.

text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich met for nearly four hours with his Republican colleagues on Monday to discuss his admitted ethics violations and party leaders predicted afterwards he will win re-election on Tuesday to his leadership post.
Four Republicans announced they will not vote for Gingrich when Congress convenes on Tuesday and others said they had not decided.

But Ohio Republican Representative John Boehner, chairman of the House Republican Conference, told reporters: "I really do expect tomorrow that there will be no question that Newt Gingrich will be the first Republican speaker re-elected in 68 years."
The meeting was the first between Gingrich and House Republicans since he acknowledged on December 21 that he broke House ethics rules.

The ethics committee, investigating charges against him for two years, is to meet on Wednesday to begin the process that will lead to a recommendation for punishment. The vote on Tuesday will be held without members knowing the outcome of the ethics case, widely expected to be a reprimand.

Earlier on Monday Rep James Leach of Iowa, chairman of the House Banking Committee, announced he would not vote for Gingrich. He was the most senior of four publicly announced defectors. The others were newcomers Linda Smith of Washington, Tom Campbell of California and Michael Forbes of New York.
Leach's office said he would vote for another, unnamed, Republican. Smith said she might vote for Leach.

If as few as 10 Republicans cast their votes for others, Gingrich would not get an overall majority and a second ballot would be required. But Boehner predicted Gingrich would win on the first ballot. Republicans control the House 227-207, with one independent who votes with the Democrats.
In a statement Leach said Gingrich was too tainted by ethics breaches to hold a post as prestigious and powerful as the speakership.

In a three-page statement, Leach said in part: "The occupant of this position must be free of any shadow concerning allegiance to the law or to the truth. Accordingly, for the country's sake I have concluded that the most responsible course of action for the speaker is to step down and for the members to choose another leader for the House."

Gingrich admitted he brought discredit to the House by not doing enough to prevent the use of tax-exempt donations in a partisan political activity -- in this case a college course he taught titled "Renewing American Civilisation" -- and by misleading ethics committee investigators looking into the matter.

Participants in the Republican meeting said members questioned Gingrich about the ethics case and Rep Henry Hyde of Illinois told reporters there were "very intense, emotional, sincere speeches" by members.
Smith said Gingrich should be defeated because the charge against him will distract from House Republicans' programme. She also said she believed more charges will be filed against him.

"We don't believe it's a hanging offence," she told reporters. "But we believe that it is big enough that it breaks down the credibility of the American people in him and I believe there will be other shoes to drop around this."
Boehner said only a few Republicans spoke against Gingrich and members wanted to know the specifics of the ethics case.
But he accused Democrats of going after the speaker. "It's a political battle. It's not an ethics case," he said.
